opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it gets at the core of what we were trying to do with the self-modifying version of Titans and, more broadly, the nested learning perspective.

In a standard Transformer, or even the original Titans, you have W_Q, W_K, and W_V. These are learned during pre-training and then frozen at test time. Every token gets projected by the same fixed matrices. The memory itself, the attention cache in a Transformer or the neural memory module in Titans, adapts to context, but the way you *write into* and *read from* that memory is fixed. So the model can store new information, but it can't change *how* it decides what's worth storing or how to address it.

A self-referential associative memory removes that asymmetry. The modules that generate the keys, the values, and even the learning rate and the retention or forgetting gate are themselves associative memories, updated in-context with their own update rules. So the model isn't only learning "what should I remember." It's also learning, at test time, "how should I produce the keys and values I use to remember." In the most self-referential form, the memory generates its own values, the targets it's trained toward. It's partly defining its own objective as it goes.

From the nested learning view, a Transformer with learned projections has two levels. The outer level is pre-training, which updates Q, K, and V slowly. The inner level is the attention or memory, which updates every token. The projections live entirely at the slow level. In the self-modifying setup, we push those projections into the fast, in-context level too. They become part of the optimization process that runs during inference, rather than parameters that only gradient descent at training time can touch.

Why does that matter? Learned Q, K, V give you a fixed coordinate system for memory, and that's a real limitation for continual learning or for long contexts where the distribution shifts. If the right notion of what counts as a key changes partway through a long document or task, a frozen projection can't follow it. A self-modifying memory can adapt its own addressing scheme, which moves us toward models that actually learn how to learn at test time, rather than just accumulating context.

So in short, learned Q, K, V means the model learned once how to build memories. Self-referential means it keeps relearning that, in context, as part of the same process.

r001.rationale: It says Q, K, and V projections are fixed at test time, but does not state that softmax attention itself does not control those projections.

r002.rationale: It does not describe applying the chain rule to a gradient descent update or deriving a recurrence analogous to linear attention.

r003.rationale: It says the memory can generate its own values, but does not identify the value component as depending on the memory’s current weight state.

r004.rationale: It says the self-modifying setup moves Q, K, and V projections into the fast in-context level, where they are part of the optimization process during inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and I think it's actually the crux of what we were trying to get at with the self-modifying Titans work. So let me try to separate the two.

In a standard model with learned Q, K, and V projections, those projections are parameters. They're learned during training, and then at test time they're frozen. Every token that comes in gets mapped through the exact same matrices. So the memory itself, the part that's actually changing as you see new context, is just the key-value state, or in the case of a recurrent or linear attention model, the recurrent state. The projections that decide how to read from and write into that memory are fixed. They were decided by gradient descent on the training set and that's it.

What we're doing with the self-referential or self-modifying version is saying: why should the projections be the thing that's frozen? If you think about memory as a learning problem, which is really the framing of Titans and the whole nested learning view, then the memory module is an inner learner. It has its own objective, something like an associative memory loss, and it's updating its parameters at test time based on the data it sees. In the original Titans, the thing being updated was the memory module, an MLP, and the keys, values, and queries were still produced by fixed projections.

The self-modifying step is to let the model generate, or update, its own projections as well. So the matrices that produce the keys, the values, even the learning rate and the forgetting signals, those are themselves outputs of the memory, or they're updated by the inner optimization. The model is effectively writing the rules for how it writes to memory. That's why we call it self-referential. The parameters that govern the update are being updated by the same process.

So the practical distinction is: in the learned-projection model, the mapping from input to key and value is the same at token one and at token one million. In the self-modifying version, that mapping has drifted, because the model has seen the context and adjusted how it wants to encode things. One nice intuition is that it's like the difference between having a fixed notebook format you fill in, versus being able to redesign the notebook as you go based on what kind of information keeps showing up.

And then the other point I'd make is that this is a different level in the hierarchy of update frequencies. The outer projections in a transformer update at the frequency of pretraining, essentially never at inference. The memory state updates every token. The self-modifying projections sit somewhere in between conceptually, they're parameters, but they're being optimized on a fast timescale. That's really the nested learning perspective: you have multiple levels of optimization running at different frequencies, and the question is which parameters you choose to put at which level.

r003.rationale: It says projections can be updated by the memory or inner optimization, but does not identify the recurrence’s value component as depending on the memory’s current weight state.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is that learning the Q, K, and V projections doesn’t, by itself, make the memory self-referential. In a standard setup, you learn those projections during training, and then at inference time they’re fixed. They determine what you query, what you use as an address, and what you want to store. The memory can still change, but the mechanism that constructs its updates is fixed.

With self-modifying Titan, the memory itself participates in producing the quantities used to update it. So the current state of the memory affects how it interprets the next input and how it changes in response. That’s the self-reference: the thing being modified also helps determine its own modification.

So I wouldn’t draw the distinction as ‘learned projections versus no learned projections.’ It’s about where those projections come from and whether the update mechanism is itself part of the evolving memory. You can have learned Q, K, and V and still have an externally specified, fixed learning rule.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is what is learned during training versus what can change as the model processes a sequence. With learned Q, K, and V projections, you learn how to construct queries, keys, and values, but those projection weights are typically fixed at inference time. The representations depend on the input; the rules for producing them don’t change.

In a self-referential associative memory, the memory participates in constructing its own update. So it’s not just storing an association between a key and a value supplied by fixed projections. Its current state helps determine what it should associate and how it should change. As the memory changes, that can change the behavior of subsequent updates.

So simply having learned Q, K, and V doesn’t make a mechanism self-referential. The question is whether those are fixed, externally learned mappings, or whether the adaptive memory itself is involved in generating the signals that modify it. That feedback loop is the important distinction.
